title: Practical usage units and commercial guidance for consumption pricing
content:
Overview

Purpose: give sales, product marketing, and finance a concise operational playbook for framing consumption-based pricing to customers: why we use token-like usage units, how to map customer workloads to those units, tier & bundle recommendations, and clear discount guardrails for commercial negotiations.

Why focus on usage units (short answer)
- Aligns value capture to actual product consumption: customers pay for the incremental inference work they run rather than a blunt seat/throughput tax.
- Preserves fairness across workloads: long-context document summarization, high-rate chat, and small embedding workloads can be measured with the same unit semantics.
- Enables predictable optimization levers: caching, batching, and quantization directly reduce unit consumption, which customers can see in their bill and in console telemetry.

Why token-ish units (why not pure requests or seats)
- Tokens approximate compute & memory footprint across different model families and sequence lengths. That makes the unit meaningful for both performance/cost and product usage.
- Simple proxies (requests or calls) break for diverse workloads: a single request for a 16k-context model can be 10x the cost of a short chat turn. Tokens normalize that.
- We recommend we present "consumption units" as a UX-friendly concept (examples below) and map them to tokens internally; avoid overwhelming customers with low-level details in early conversations.

Operational definition: Redwood consumption unit (RCU)
- Base definition: 1 RCU = 1k model tokens processed (sum of prompt + response tokens) normalized by model family weight.
- Model-family weight: small multiplier per model class to reflect relative GPU cost (e.g., medium-7B: 1.0, large-30B: 2.6, quantized variants get discount factors).
- Example: 3k tokens on large-30B => 3 * 2.6 = 7.8 RCUs.
- Presentation: Display "RCUs consumed" in billing and per-route dashboards; show both raw tokens and RCUs for advanced customers.

Mapping customer workloads to units (sales cheat-sheet)
- Short chat (interactive): 40–150 tokens/turn => ~0.04–0.15 RCUs per turn on medium models. Good framing: "~1k turns per $X/month" for quick math.
- Long document summarization (batch): 8k–40k tokens => 8–40 RCUs (medium) or 20–104 RCUs (large). Frame as "cost per document" where possible.
- Embeddings: charge per 1k vectors or per 1k tokens used for input? Recommend: separate embeddings meter (1 RCU per 1k embedding vectors normalized). Keep embedding unit distinct to avoid confusion.
- Reranking / search pipelines: account for both embed + model scoring; provide sample templates customers can paste into the console to estimate spend.

Tiering and bundles (recommended structure)
- Free / Trial tier: 10k RCUs and 5k embed vectors free credits over 30 days. Purpose: rapid prototyping and demoing latency-dependent UX.
- Starter: pay-as-you-go with no commitment, base price per RCU (public price). Target: early-stage teams and experimentation.
- Scale: committed monthly spend (3–12 month), discounted RCU price, access to Dedicated capacity trials and prioritized support. Target: SMB/scaleups.
- Enterprise: annual committed capacity, reserved RCU blocks with burst credits, private deployment options, and SLAs. Price per RCU substantially lower; include Managed onboarding credits.
- Add-on: embeddings allotment (separate unit and price), and Dedicated capacity seat for high-throughput predictable pipelines.

Naming guidance (marketing friendly)
- Use user-focused names not technical: e.g., "Starter (Prototype)", "Scale (Production)", "Enterprise (Dedicated)". Avoid model family names in tier titles.

Discounting guardrails (commercial rules)
- Baseline concept: discounts should reflect committed predictable revenue and reduced marginal cost when customers move off hosted burst usage (reserved GPU pools).
- Typical discount bands (examples for Sales calibration):
  - No commitment: 0–5% promotions only for short-term campaigns.
  - 3–6 month commitment: 8–15% depending on volume.
  - 12 month commitment / ARR minimum: 20–35% depending on unit economics and add-ons.
  - Strategic enterprise deals: up to 45% with guaranteed minimums, longer contract terms, and platform/implementation fees.
- Non-price concessions: prefer operational concessions (longer onboarding, SSO integrations, extended telemetry retention) over rounding discounts.
- Seat-equivalency trade: If signing a seat-based support bundle, treat it as additive to committed spend rather than substitutive for RCU discounts.

Negotiation playbook for AE & Commercials
- If prospect pushes for flat per-request pricing: demonstrate three representative workloads with RCUs and show delta; emphasize how tokens reflect compute.
- For price-seeking customers: offer transient credit for migration (one-time) + a gradual ramp to committed tier pricing.
- When customers ask to reframe as seats: translate seats -> expected RCUs using observed customer signals (requests/day, avg tokens). Provide a 3-month forecast template.
- Discount approval matrix: frontline AE can approve up to 10% for ARR < $100k, Sales Director for 10–25%, VP/Sales for >25% or strategic concessions. Finance must sign off on >30% discounts.

Message scripts (short battlecards)
- Engineering-skeptical customer: "Tokens let us mirror the actual GPU work your requests do. That means you only pay for what you run, and optimization steps like KV caching or quantized models directly reduce your bill."
- CFO / Procurement: "Consumption pricing aligns spend to actual usage. For predictable needs we recommend reserved blocks to get lower unit economics and predictable monthly charges."
- Product lead worried about complexity: "We show both high-level \"consumption units\" and the underlying token math in the console. You can opt for simple estimates in procurement and dig into token detail later."

Competitive positioning (how to beat incumbents)
- Against pure seat models: emphasize fairness and pay-for-what-you-use; show cost modeling for representative customers to reveal hidden costs of seat-only pricing.
- Against simplistic per-request vendors: showcase long-tail scenarios (long contexts, multi-step pipelines) where per-call hides variance.
- Against token-only vendors: we win on tooling & visibility — show per-route breakdown, model-family normalization, and optimization recommendations in console.

Operational items for product & billing
- Console: default display RCUs + raw tokens; include a calculator that converts sample prompts to monthly spend.
- Exports: provide CSV with per-request tokens, model family weight, and RCUs so customers can verify bills.
- Alerts: set thresholds for sudden RCU rate increases and auto-suggest optimizations.
- Reporting: weekly summary of heavy consumers per customer for AE outreach.

Open questions & follow-ups
- Validate model-family weight multipliers with bench tests across the most used models.
- Decide final embedding unit (tokens vs vectors) and pricing parity. Recommendation for next step: run 10 representative customer workloads through the billing simulator and refine weights+examples.

Appendix: quick examples
- 1k chat turns at 100 tokens avg on medium model: 0.1 RCU/turn => 100 RCUs/month. If price = $0.05/RCU => $5/month.
- 1000 long DOC summaries (20k tokens) on large model: 20 RCUs * 2.6 weight * 1000 = 52,000 RCUs => $2,600 at $0.05/RCU (or discounted rate for commitment).

End of doc — feedback requested from Finance, Product Pricing, and Solutions Eng for a follow-on worked example packet.
